The Black turnstone (Arenaria melanocephala) is a medium-sized shorebird that breeds along the rocky coastlines of Alaska and winters along the Pacific coast of North America. Eggs are incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] and hatch after approximately 21.5 days [ab = approximately 21.5 days], a developmental period typical of many charadriiform species. Newly hatched chicks emerge with a wet weight at birth averaging 12.6 grams [Wwb = 12.6 grams], a modest mass that reflects the energetic constraints of yolk-dependent development in this lineage. This initial body size is comparable to that reported for the congeneric ruddy turnstone (Arenaria interpres), though subtle differences in neonatal provisioning have been noted across populations. The downy chicks are precocial and leave the nest within hours of hatching, though they remain dependent on parental brooding for thermoregulation during the first several days of life, a period during which they must quickly gain mass to improve their chances of survival in the cold, windswept intertidal habitats that characterize the species' breeding range along the Bering Sea coast.

Field studies conducted during the breeding season on the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta have documented female body mass at the onset of incubation. This measurement is taken shortly after arrival on the breeding grounds, when body condition is typically at its seasonal peak. Males tend to be slightly smaller than females in this species, a pattern of reverse sexual size dimorphism that is common among the Scolopacidae. Sexual maturity is attained considerably later, with puberty occurring 63 days after hatching [tp = 63 days after hatching], a delay that reflects the time required to complete somatic growth and accumulate sufficient reserves for reproductive effort at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. The age at first successful brood is 2 years since birth [tR = 2 years since birth], indicating that these birds do not breed during their first full summer but defer reproduction until their second year, consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes survival and experience over early reproduction in a highly seasonal environment where resource availability is unpredictable at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C].
